doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

chapter: Songwriting craft and the blues form
title: Blues limitations, major sevenths and Bruce Iglauer
summary: Blues is open and limited like haiku; she snuck in a major seventh despite Iglauer's rule, and limits give a different kind of freedom.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well let’s see what I got with me. You take credit? Yeah you mentioned that, the idea of writing a blues song if you’re not suffering.
Right. Right. Well actually that was an inspiration for a song.
Yeah. Well that’s what I love about the blues is that it’s so, you can do whatever you want with it.

It’s very, very open. And people, of course I write stuff that’s not that A-A-B form all the time. But people say, “How can you write blues?” My jazz friends say, “Oh it’s so dull, it’s so limited.” And I say, “Are you familiar with Haiku?”
Because you have limitations. And even if the form isn’t that A-A-B form, there are chords you would almost never use in blues like major seventh I guess is what it’s called, right? Is that right?
I’ve done it though. Bruce Iglauer said, “I will never have a major seven on my label.” And I threw one in. Anyway.
What a funny thing to say.
Well yeah, but I mean I know what he means. It’s very loungy.
Yeah, so there are limitations. And I love them.
People think that freedom is such a good thing sometimes, but I think it sometimes makes it harder. Too much freedom is hard to deal with it.

Yeah. Well having limitations gives you a different kind of freedom. You don’t have to — it’s like having a great bass player like I’ve had the last few days. And a great drummer. There are things I don’t have to think about. So that frees me up to think about other things.
